source.title: Are Your Reasoning Models Reasoning or Guessing? A Mechanistic Analysis of Hierarchical Reasoning Models

record.tranche_reason: The paper uses “grokking” for changes across inference-time reasoning segments, not delayed generalization during training after overfitting. It does not test the claim versions’ training dynamics or other specified mechanisms.
record.gate_note: The reported grokking-like result is about loss changing across HRM’s inference-time segments on Sudoku, not training accuracy saturating before test accuracy improves. The Sudoku accuracy results for augmentation and bootstrapping, and the fixed-point analyses, do not measure the delayed-generalization behavior in the claim.
record.test_reason: The paper borrows the word "grokking" as an analogy for an abrupt per-sample loss drop across HRM's inference-time recursion segments on Sudoku-Extreme. It does not measure train vs. test accuracy over training steps, delayed generalization after overfitting, circuit formation, weight decay, dataset-size effects or optimizer artifacts. No result bears on any version (V1–V7) of the training-time grokking claim.
record.authors_conclusion: Correct. The authors conclude that HRM "guesses" rather than reasons: individual trajectories plateau near spurious fixed points and then abruptly succeed, or stay trapped. They also report fixed-point violations on very simple puzzles, which data mixing fixes. Combining data mixing, input relabeling and checkpoint bootstrapping raises Sudoku-Extreme accuracy from 55.0% to 96.9%.
record.recipe_differences: The study analyzes latent-state trajectories and inference-time segment losses in HRM on Sudoku and maze tasks; it does not reproduce the training-time grokking method in the cited original sources.
record.method_sensitivity: The paper reports different segment-loss patterns for averaged test samples versus individual samples, and distinguishes successful from failed individual cases.

fits_no_version.finding: Averaged over test samples, HRM segment loss falls smoothly with segment depth. Per sample, loss plateaus and then drops abruptly to zero, or stays on the plateau and the sample fails.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: In recursive latent reasoning models, per-sample progress across inference steps is abrupt (attractor escape) even though the averaged progress looks gradual.

record.problems: The segment-wise loss findings are primarily qualitative and presented in figures; the text gives no uncertainty estimates for them. They concern inference-time trajectories rather than the claim’s training-time delayed-generalization behavior.
record.rows_left_out: No results bearing on the claim versions were omitted. Other reported Sudoku and Maze-Hard accuracy comparisons concern augmentation and bootstrapping performance, not delayed generalization after overfitting.

untested.parts: No training-time train vs. test accuracy curves, delay, or training-set-size dependence.
No tracking of a generalizing circuit or removal of memorization during training.
No non-algorithmic data and no initialization-scale or weight-norm manipulation.
No weight-decay, critical dataset size or ungrokking analysis.
No comparison of algorithms across runs. Checkpoint bootstrapping shows that adjacent checkpoints solve different samples, but it does not identify algorithms.

record.verdict_notes: The "grokking" in this paper is terminological borrowing applied to inference-time recursion, not to training dynamics. The reader's T6/discusses classification stands. The Section 4.1 remark that the loss reduction rate across segments grows over training is also not a delayed-generalization measure.

versions.untested_parts: The study does not test training accuracy versus test accuracy over training, delayed generalization after overfitting, or how the delay varies with training-set size.
It does not track formation of a generalizing circuit or removal of memorizing components during training. Its segment-wise loss results concern inference-time recursion.
No non-algorithmic datasets or initialization-scale or weight-norm sweeps are tested.
No LLM pretraining or fine-tuning on realistic data is tested.
No weight-decay or low-norm efficiency account, critical dataset size, or ungrokking result is tested.
The study does not compare whether runs converge to the same identifiable algorithm.
No adaptive-optimizer instability or floating-point softmax artifact is tested.

rows.subject: HRM
rows.operation_detail: Measured segment-wise loss averaged across Sudoku-Extreme test samples.
rows.value: figure only; text says more segments produce smoothly smaller loss on average, and the loss reduction rate increases as training progresses
rows.note: This is an inference-segment loss pattern, not delayed test-accuracy generalization after training overfit.
rows.check: Inference-segment loss averaged over test samples (Fig. 4); not a training-time train/test generalization measure. The link to no version is correct.

rows.subject: HRM
rows.operation_detail: Measured per-sample loss across inference segments for successful cases.
rows.value: figure only; text describes a lengthy plateau followed by a sudden drop to zero
rows.note: The reported transition occurs across inference segments, not across training steps.
rows.check: Per-sample plateau-then-drop occurs across inference segments, not training steps (Fig. 5). The link to no version is correct.

rows.subject: HRM
rows.operation_detail: Measured per-sample loss across inference segments for failure cases.
rows.value: figure only; text says loss can remain on a plateau for the rest of the reasoning segments and the sample fails
rows.note: This is persistent inference-time error, not evidence about train/test accuracy dynamics.
rows.check: Failure cases stay on a plateau across inference segments. This is not delayed generalization during training; the link to no version is correct.
